text.p: Swedish vehicle maker AB Volvo on Wednesday posted a nine percent rise in pre-tax profits in 1996 and proposed a redemption of its own shares with one for each multiple of 20 Volvo shares held.
Volvo said a positive currency effect of 800 million crowns ($107.6 million) boosted its 1996 operating profits as it reported a pre-tax profit of 14.20 billion crowns. ($ = 7.435 Swedish Crowns)
The result was largely in line with market expectations with analysts expecting a profit of 13.6 billion crowns and the share price showed little movement, trading one higher at 181 crowns.
"Overall the results achieved in 1996 show that much remains to be done to raise Volvo's profitability and stabilise it on a consistently high level," chief executive Soren Gyll said in a statement.
In 1996 Volvo posted a slip in sales to 156.06 billion crowns from 171.51 billion crowns.
Volvo Truck's income was worst hit, due primarily to a loss in the North American truck operations, as already well known in the market.
The unit's sales fell 13 percent to 44.28 billion crowns and operating profit slumped to 878 million crowns from 5.07 billion crowns.
"Volvo Trucks experienced sharply reduced demand and substantial losses in North America," Gyll said.
"A comprehensive restructuring programme that was advanced will not have full impact on earnings until this year."
Volvo Bus also reported weaker operating income due to increased competition and problems in South America, even though it delivered eight percent more buses totalling 7,410 units.
But Gyll said these operations have been rationalised with appreciable results in terms of reducing costs.
Elsewhere the company was happy with its performance.
"The trend of income in Volvo Cars was favourable and Volvo Construction Equipment continued to show good operating income," the company said.
Volvo Cars sales were flat at 83.59 billion crowns with the number of cars invoiced slipping to 368,300 from 374,600. Its operating profit rose to 1.50 billion crowns from 1.09 billion crowns.
Volvo announced that since the repurchase of its own shares was not currently possible by Swedish law its board was proposing a redemption of its own shares with one share for each group of 20 held.
The price will be based on the market price plus a premium.
"The board's ambition is to implement the redemption procedure as soon as possible," Volvo said.
It said the schedule and terms would be disclosed by the latest when Volvo publishes its annual report on March 19.
Volvo proposed a dividend of 4.30 crowns a share for 1996 compared to 4.00 crowns in 1995 when one share of Swedish Match was also handed out for every Volvo share held.
-- Belinda Goldsmith, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700-1045
